overview.text: Inertia is matter’s tendency to resist a change in its motion: an object at rest stays at rest, while one already moving continues in a straight line at constant speed unless a net external force acts. This principle is stated in Newton’s first law, also called the law of inertia, and explains why motion can continue without a continuing push. Everyday objects often slow because friction or drag supplies an external force, not because inertia makes them stop. More massive objects have greater inertia, so their motion is harder to change; mass measures inertia and, unlike weight, does not depend on location or gravity.

key_facts.text: With no net external force, an object at rest remains at rest.
An object in motion keeps a constant velocity—a straight path at constant speed—unless a net external force acts.
Friction and drag can slow moving objects; inertia itself is not what makes them stop.
Greater mass means greater inertia, making an object’s motion harder to change.
Newton’s laws describe how inertia behaves, but do not explain its underlying nature.
